segments.t: At the agency, Mathias hosts a party to celebrate acquiring the book rights to a novel about disabled animals. Noemie is appalled when Mathias begins to mock the author and her cause in front of the whole room. Let's listen to their tense exchange in French first.
Qu'est-ce qui se passe ici?
On fête ça! Bois un verre!
Je peux te dire un mot?
Oui, bien sûr, ma chérie.
Tu n'as pas utilisé mes secrets?
Non, écoute, je te le promets.
Tu le jures devant tout le monde?
Je voudrais porter un grand toast!
À tous les animaux handicapés!
Sans eux, pas de droits!
J'ai enfin lu ce livre!
C'est dingue, c'est n'importe quoi!
Mathias, tu me dégoûtes vraiment!
Noémie, attends, reviens tout de suite!
Let's examine the conversation line by line and explore the French expressions.
Qu'est-ce qui se passe ici?
'What is going on here?' Noemie arrives at the agency and wonders what the celebration is about. The question phrase 'qu'est-ce qui' asks what.
On fête ça! Bois un verre!
'We are celebrating! Have a drink!' Mathias pours champagne to mark their latest victory. The verb 'are celebrating' means to celebrate.
Je peux te dire un mot?
'Can I have a word with you?' Noemie quietly pulls Mathias aside to ask a serious question. The expression 'to say' means to have a brief word.
Oui, bien sûr, ma chérie.
'Yes, of course, my darling.' Mathias answers her with his usual warm charm. The phrase 'of course' means of course.
Tu n'as pas utilisé mes secrets?
'You did not use my secrets?' Noemie worries that Mathias exploited her private confessions. The negative construction 'not' frames the past tense verb.
Non, écoute, je te le promets.
'No, listen, I promise you.' Mathias reassures his assistant with a straight face. The verb 'promise' means to give one's word.
Tu le jures devant tout le monde?
'Do you swear in front of everyone?' Noemie insists on an explicit commitment. The prepositional phrase 'devant tout le monde' means in front of everybody.
Je voudrais porter un grand toast!
'I would like to propose a big toast!' Mathias turns to the crowd and raises his glass. The polite conditional 'I' expresses a desire.
À tous les animaux handicapés!
'To all the handicapped animals!' Mathias dedicates the toast with blatant mockery. The adjective 'handicapped' modifies the plural noun 'animals'.
Sans eux, pas de droits!
'Without them, no rights!' Mathias jokes about how the cause brought them the adaptation deal. The preposition 'without' denotes absence or lack.
J'ai enfin lu ce livre!
'I finally read this book!' Mathias admits that he has only just skimmed the manuscript. The adverb 'finally' means at last or finally.
C'est dingue, c'est n'importe quoi!
'It is crazy, it makes no sense!' Mathias openly mocks the content of the novel. The idiom 'n'importe quoi' denotes complete nonsense.
Mathias, tu me dégoûtes vraiment!
'Mathias, you really disgust me!' Noemie is appalled by his utter cynicism and lack of respect. The verb 'disgust' expresses intense aversion.
Noémie, attends, reviens tout de suite!

'Noemie, wait, come back immediately!' Mathias calls after her in surprise as she storms out. The imperative 'wait' urges someone to stop and listen. Now let's listen to the complete discussion once more to reinforce the vocabulary.

Disgusted by Mathias's cruelty and broken promises, Noemie storms out of the party in tears. Meanwhile at ASK, Camille learns of her father's scheme and resolves to handle the situation herself. Now let's listen to the complete scene one last time.
